Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Energy Corp. Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Lisa Chen, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Lisa Chen: Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex Energy Corp.'s Q2 2024 earnings call. Joining me on the call today are Mike Harlan, Chief Executive Officer; John Ramirez, Chief Financial Officer; Sarah Jenkins, Chief Operating Officer; Tom Rivera, VP of Exploration; Elena Vasquez, VP of Marketing; and Dr. Rachel Kim, Chief Sustainability Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we make today may be forward-looking. These statements are based on current expectations and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks.

I will now turn the call over to Mike Harlan.

Mike Harlan: Thank you, Lisa, and good morning, everyone. Apex Energy Corp. delivered solid results in Q2 2024, driven by strong operational performance and favorable commodity prices. We achieved robust production growth with total volumes averaging around 500,000 BOE per day, reflecting key well results and efficiencies across our portfolio. I'm particularly pleased with our progress on lifting costs per BOE, which continued their downward trend through targeted initiatives. We are focused on maintaining disciplined capital expenditure guidance, outlining future spending plans that balance growth and returns. Further, we are working on optimizing debt levels, with total debt, net debt, and leverage ratios showing meaningful improvement. We continue to adjust to proved reserves additions, boasting a reserve replacement ratio well above industry averages through organic growth. We are advancing production guidance for the next quarter and full year, factoring in operational tailwinds and risks. Finally, we are taking steps to enhance exploration and drilling activities, with standout well performances setting the stage for future plans.

Now, I'll turn the call over to John Ramirez to discuss our financial results in more detail.

John Ramirez: Thank you, Mike. As Mike mentioned, we had a strong quarter. Our revenue was $2.8 billion, up 25% year-over-year. Operating income was $1.2 billion, and net income was $900 million. We generated $600 million in free cash flow and returned $400 million to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases. Our balance sheet remains strong, with $6.8 billion in debt and $1.4 billion in cash.

Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. I'll now turn to our capital expenditure guidance, where we'll outline our disciplined spending plans for 2025 and beyond, along with the expected returns that underpin our capital allocation framework. As you know, we've maintained a fortress balance sheet here at Apex Energy Corp., with net debt to EBITDAX below 0.5x, giving us the flexibility to invest in our high-return inventory while returning significant capital to shareholders via our $1.2 billion buyback authorization and 12% dividend yield.

Let me start with a quick recap of 2024. We deployed $2.6 billion in capex, coming in at the low end of our initial $2.5 to $2.8 billion guidance, thanks to operational efficiencies like our 15% reduction in D&C costs per foot in the Permian Delaware Basin. This resulted in full-year production of 450,000 BOE/d, up 8% year-over-year, with oil representing 68% of our mix.

Looking ahead, we're guiding 2025 capex to $2.9 to $3.1 billion, a modest 12% increase at the midpoint, weighted 75% toward development, 15% exploration, and 10% base maintenance and infrastructure. This reflects our commitment to capital discipline amid a WTI forward curve averaging $78/bbl and Henry Hub at $3.20/MMBtu—scenarios that deliver robust free cash flow of $1.4 to $1.6 billion at those prices, assuming no major service cost inflation.

Breaking it down by category and region:

First, development capex, our largest bucket at $2.2 to $2.3 billion. In the Permian Basin—where we hold 250,000 net acres in the core Delaware and Midland sub-basins—we're allocating $1.5 billion to drill 140 net wells, focusing on our Wolfcamp A and Bone Springs stacks. We've extended lateral lengths to an average 14,500 feet, up from 12,000 last year, with proppant intensity at 2,500 lbs/ft and hybrid slickwater fracs incorporating our proprietary diverter tech. This drives first-year EURs of 1.8 MBOE per well, with type-curve IRRs exceeding 55% at $75 WTI and half-cycle paybacks under 10 months. We're running six operated rigs steady-state, with D&C cycle times down to 95 days, mirroring efficiencies seen at peers like Pioneer and Occidental.

In the Eagle Ford, $400 million supports 35 net wells targeting our oil window in Karnes and DeWitt counties. Here, we're layering in our first hybrid completions with 40/70 mesh sand, boosting IP30s by 15% to 1,400 BOE/d, yielding 45% IRRs and strong hedges at $75 Brent equivalent.

Exploration capex ramps to $430 to $480 million, including two Final Investment Decisions—or FIDs—in the deepwater Gulf of Mexico. Our Winterfell prospect in Green Canyon mirrors Chevron's Anchor project dynamics: high-pressure, high-temp reservoirs with Vaca Muerta-like shale potential. We're budgeting $250 million for a 2025 spud, with pre-drill NPV10 of $800 million on a 40 MMBOE resource, targeting 60% IRR post-sanction. Onshore, $150 million funds appraisal in the Uinta Basin, where our Duchesne discovery mirrors the Womack Hill play—tight oil with 30-degree API gravity and initial GORs under 1,000 scf/bbl. Early flow tests hit 1,200 BOPD from 5,000-foot laterals, de-risking 50 locations at 40-50% IRRs.

Maintenance and infrastructure at $290 to $310 million includes electrification of our Permian pads—saving 20% on fuel costs via grid tie-ins—and midstream bolt-ons like our $100 million stake in a Matterhorn Express-like NGL pipeline expansion to Corpus Christi. We're also advancing CCUS pilots, injecting 500,000 tonnes CO2 annually into our Salado Formation saline aquifer under 45Q credits, positioning us for IRA incentives akin to Occidental's STRATOS project.

Regionally, 65% of spend stays in the Lower 48 Permian for its unmatched returns—our Midland inventory supports 10+ years at 300,000 BOE/d pace. Eagle Ford adds low-risk growth, Gulf exploration high-upside optionality, and we're pausing international bids amid Guyana's fiscal creep and OPEC+ cuts. No M&A planned unless accretive at sub-5x EV/EBITDA multiples, like our 2023 $2.5 billion Delaware tuck-in.

On returns, our portfolio threshold is 40% IRR and 2x NPV10 payback at $65 WTI floor. 2025 program averages 52% IRR, up from 48% in 2024, driven by tech like digital twins for frac optimization—reducing screen-outs by 30%—and AI-driven sweet-spot mapping via our partnership with SLB's Delfi platform. Sensitivities: +$5 WTI adds $400 million FCF; gas at $3.50/MMBtu lifts Eagle Ford returns 5 points. We're hedging 60% of 2025 oil at $76/bbl swaps to lock in returns.

Strategically, this guidance balances growth—targeting 8-10% production CAGR to 520,000 BOE/d by 2027—with ROCE expansion to 18%. In a world of Brent volatility from Red Sea disruptions and non-OPEC supply like Brazil's Buzios, we're prioritizing Tier 1 inventory over volume chasing, much like ConocoPhillips' playbook. This de-risks our 15-year runway while advancing net-zero ambitions through electrification and methane abatement—our Leak Detection program hit 0.05% methane intensity last quarter.

Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining our Q3 earnings call for Apex Energy Corp. As we wrap up a strong quarter with WTI averaging $82 per barrel and Brent at $86, driven by sustained OPEC+ cuts and robust global demand, I'd like to turn to our balance sheet, which remains a cornerstone of our financial resilience. Our disciplined capital allocation has continued to fortify our liquidity position, enabling us to navigate the volatility inherent in upstream oil and gas while positioning us for opportunistic growth. Let me dive into the key metrics on debt levels, net debt, and leverage ratios.

Starting with total debt, we ended the quarter with consolidated total debt of $6.8 billion, comprising $4.2 billion in long-term senior notes, $1.9 billion in term loans, and $0.7 billion in short-term borrowings under our revolving credit facility. This represents a 12% year-over-year reduction from $7.7 billion at Q3 last year, primarily driven by $850 million in debt repayments funded by our record free cash flow generation of $1.2 billion in the first nine months. Notably, we opportunistically refinanced $1.5 billion of our 2024-dated 6.125% senior notes with new 10-year issuance at 5.25%—a 90 basis point savings amid the recent tightening of high-yield spreads to 350 bps over Treasuries. This not only extends our maturity profile, with a weighted average tenor now at 4.8 years and no major maturities until 2026, but also locks in favorable rates ahead of potential Fed pivots.

Our liquidity remains robust, with $1.4 billion in unrestricted cash and equivalents and $2.1 billion of undrawn capacity under our $4.5 billion syndicated revolver, backed by 55 participating banks including JPMorgan and BofA. Utilization sits at just 15%, giving us ample dry powder for D&C programs or bolt-on M&A in the Permian.

Moving to net debt, which we define as total debt minus cash and cash equivalents—a metric we believe best reflects our deleveraging progress—this stood at $5.4 billion at quarter-end, down 18% from $6.6 billion a year ago. This $1.2 billion reduction was fueled by several tailwinds: first, Permian Basin outperformance, where our 120-rig development program in the Delaware and Midland basins generated $900 million in excess cash flow at sub-$45 WTI breakevens; second, selective non-core asset monetizations, including the $450 million divestiture of our legacy North Sea interests to Harbour Energy, which were fully impaired last cycle; and third, our disciplined hedging book covering 65% of 2024 oil production at $75 WTI floors via collars and fixed swaps with counterparties like BP and Shell. Regionally, this net debt snap reflects strength in our U.S. onshore assets offsetting ramp-up capex in high-return Guyana waters, where our Liza Phase 2 FPSO came online ahead of schedule, boosting FPSO utilization to 95% and contributing $200 million in incremental cash flow.

Now, on leverage ratios, our net debt to trailing twelve-month EBITDAX—a key covenant metric under our credit agreement—improved to 1.1x from 1.6x at year-end 2023 and 2.3x at the 2022 trough. This puts us well below our 2.5x covenant ceiling and firmly on track for our year-end target of sub-1.0x, aligning with investment-grade peers like ConocoPhillips at 0.8x. Gross debt to EBITDAX sits at 1.4x, while our debt-to-capitalization ratio of 28% underscores a healthy equity buffer, with book equity at $17.2 billion after $300 million in share repurchases under our $1 billion program. From a credit perspective, we've seen our corporate family rating affirmed at BB+ by S&P with a positive outlook, reflecting our counter-cyclical debt reduction strategy—much like EOG Resources' playbook during the 2021 recovery.

Strategically, these metrics enable us to prioritize returns to shareholders while funding organic growth. We've deployed 60% of our $3.2 billion 2024 capex budget—skewed 70/20/10 toward Permian development, Guyana appraisal, and Bakken maintenance—while committing $750 million to dividends and buybacks. Looking forward, we expect another $1.5 billion in debt paydown in 2025, targeting net leverage below 0.8x amid projected $5 billion in levered free cash flow at $75 WTI. Initiatives like our $100 million AI-optimized frac design in the Permian, reducing cycle times by 15%, and joint ventures with Petrobras in pre-salt Brazil will further enhance cash conversion cycles.

Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining our call. I'm excited to dive into our proved reserves performance, which underscores the strength of our organic growth engine and our disciplined capital allocation in this dynamic Oil & Gas landscape. As you know, proved reserves – our SEC-defined 1P inventory – are the lifeblood of long-term value creation, and we've delivered exceptional results here.

Let me start with the headline numbers for full-year 2023. We added 142 million barrels of oil equivalent (MMboe) to our proved developed producing (PDP) and proved undeveloped (PUD) reserves, net of 98 MMboe of annual production. This translates to a stellar reserve replacement ratio (RRR) of 145% – well above our long-term target of 120% and the industry's median of around 110%, per recent Wood Mackenzie data. Even more impressively, our organic RRR – excluding any M&A contributions – came in at 138%, reflecting pure execution from the drillbit and technical revisions.

To put this in context, our year-end 2023 proved reserves totaled 1.85 billion boe, up 8% from 1.71 billion boe at the end of 2022. This marks our third straight year of double-digit organic reserve growth, reversing the multi-decade industry trend of reserve attrition amid maturing basins. We've now replaced over 420% of our production on a three-year cumulative organic basis – a metric that positions us favorably against peers like Pioneer Natural Resources or Occidental, who posted organic RRRs closer to 110-120% in their last reports.

Breaking down the additions: Exploratory discoveries and extensions accounted for 65 MMboe (46% of total), driven by successful delineation in high-impact plays. Positive technical revisions added 52 MMboe (37%), primarily from better-than-expected well performance and reservoir modeling. The balance came from improved economics on existing PUDs, thanks to lower breakevens and higher commodity prices – WTI averaged $78/bbl in 2023, supporting conversions. Notably, negative revisions were minimal at just 8 MMboe, or 0.4% of our PDP base, far below the industry norm of 2-5%.

Regionally, our U.S. onshore assets were the powerhouse. In the Permian Basin, where we hold 650,000 net acres across the Delaware and Midland sub-basins, we booked 78 MMboe of additions – including 45 MMboe from our Wolfcamp C and Bone Springs extensions. Horizontal laterals averaging 12,500 feet, combined with our proprietary 'ApexFrac' diverter tech – which boosted initial production (IP) rates by 15% over 2022 vintages – unlocked stacked pay zones previously deemed sub-economic. This pushed our Permian inventory to over 1.2 billion boe 2P, with more than 4,000 drilling locations at sub-$40/bbl breakevens. Year-over-year, Permian organic RRR hit 165%, outpacing EOG Resources' recent quarterly figures.

Shifting offshore, our Gulf of Mexico (GoM) deepwater portfolio contributed 42 MMboe, highlighted by the sidetrack success at our Loki prospect in Green Canyon Block 298, mirroring ExxonMobil's Guyana-style upside. Here, 4D seismic reprocessing and ocean-bottom node (OBN) surveys de-risked 250 MMboe of contingent resources, converting 30% to proved. GoM RRR was 210%, fueled by lower F&D costs of $4.50/boe – half the basin average – thanks to our tie-back strategy to existing infrastructure like the Marcus Hook hub.

Internationally, we added 22 MMboe in our Suriname Block 58 venture (non-operated, 20% working interest), where the recent Roystone-1 appraisal well confirmed a 500 MMboe column, akin to the Hess-Exxon Stabroek block discoveries. This is early innings, but our organic growth here supports a 10-year runway at current paces.

On the technical front, organic growth wasn't accidental. We invested $180 million in subsurface tech last year – including machine learning-driven petrophysical modeling and full-waveform inversion (FWI) seismic – which improved success rates from 72% to 85% on exploration wells. Enhanced oil recovery (EOR) pilots, like CO2 miscible flooding in our legacy Texas Panhandle fields, added 12 MMboe via performance revisions, with pilot EURs up 25%. These initiatives kept our three-year average F&D cost at $8.20/boe, 30% below the EIA's upstream peer median.

Strategically, this reserve book fortifies our free cash flow machine. With 65% of additions in Tier 1 assets (half-cycle returns >60% at $70/bbl), we're derisking into a lower-carbon future – 40% of new PUDs are electrification-ready. Looking ahead, we see 150-170 MMboe of annual organic additions through the decade, maintaining RRR above 130% even at $60/bbl. This supports our progressive dividend growth and $5-7 billion buyback authorization, while preserving balance sheet flexibility amid OPEC+ volatility and the energy transition.

Thank you, Mike, and good morning, everyone. I'll now turn to our production outlook for the third quarter and the balance of the year, along with the key factors shaping these projections. As you know, our guidance reflects a disciplined approach to capital allocation amid a volatile macro environment, with WTI averaging around $78 per barrel year-to-date and Brent holding steady above $82, supported by ongoing OPEC+ cuts and robust global demand from Asia.

For Q3 2024, we are guiding production to 510,000 to 520,000 boe per day, representing a 2% sequential increase from Q2's actuals of approximately 500,000 boe/d. Oil volumes are expected to comprise 62% of the mix, or roughly 320,000 barrels per day, with natural gas liquids at 18% and gas at 20%. This modest quarter-over-quarter growth is driven primarily by our high-return D&C program in the Permian Basin, where we've brought online 25 new Wolfcamp and Bone Springs wells since Q2, averaging initial production rates of over 1,800 boe/d per well—up 15% from last year's vintage thanks to optimized proppant designs and longer laterals exceeding 12,000 feet.

Turning to the full-year 2024 guidance, we are narrowing and raising the range to 515,000 to 525,000 boe/d, up from our prior midpoint of 505,000 boe/d. This implies full-year growth of about 8% over 2023, positioning us at the upper end of our long-term 5-10% CAGR target through 2027. Quarter four is expected to accelerate to 525,000 to 535,000 boe/d as we lap Q4 2023 turnaround impacts and realize full-cycle contributions from our Eagle Ford inventory.

Let me unpack the key factors influencing these projections, starting with the positives. Operationally, our Permian assets—now 55% of total production—are firing on all cylinders. We've reduced D&C cycle times by 20% through our ApexFlow digital platform, which integrates real-time seismic data and machine learning for precise frac staging. This has boosted our Permian inventory efficiency to 450,000 lateral feet per rig annually, outpacing peers like Pioneer and Occidental. In the Eagle Ford, we're seeing a 12% uplift from our refracturing pilots on 150 legacy wells, converting marginal Tier 2 acreage into Tier 1 economics with EURs north of 800 Mboe per well.

Regionally, our Gulf of Mexico portfolio, including our 30% stake in the Shenzi field akin to Chevron's Anchor project, will contribute incrementally as we complete subsea tie-backs ahead of hurricane season. Internationally, the ramp-up at our Suriname Block 58 offshore development—mirroring ExxonMobil's Stabroek success—adds 15,000 boe/d by year-end, with first oil now on track for Q4 following positive flow tests averaging 5,000 bbl/d per well.

Strategically, we're leveraging our $2.1 billion capex budget—65% D&C, 20% base maintenance, and 15% tech and CCS pilots—to prioritize sub-$40 WTI half-cycle returns. We've hedged 60% of our oil volumes at $75 for the back half, insulating cash flows even if WTI dips toward $70 on potential demand softening from China's slowdown.

On the risk side, we face some near-term headwinds. Q3 includes planned turnarounds at our Rockies gas plants, deferring about 10,000 boe/d, and we're monitoring Hurricane Beryl's aftermath, which could pressure Gulf uptime to 92% versus our base 95%. Supply chain constraints on Tier 3 sand have pushed Permian costs up 5% QoQ, though our multi-year contracts with U.S. Silica mitigate this. Broader risks include EIA-projected U.S. rig counts stabilizing at 580—down 5% YoY—and regulatory hurdles like the BLM's updated methane rules, which we're addressing via our $150 million electrification initiative to cut flaring 40% by 2025.

Looking ahead, these projections embed conservative assumptions: flat service costs, no M&A bolt-ons beyond our recent $400 million non-operated Permian tuck-in, and LNG export demand supporting gas realizations above $2.50/MMBtu. We're well-positioned for upside from AI-driven reservoir modeling, which recent pilots show could add 5-7% to recovery factors in our Delaware shales.

Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining our Q2 2024 earnings call. Before diving into the financials, I'd like to walk you through our operational performance, starting with production volumes, which remain the cornerstone of our value creation in this volatile market. As you know, we're reporting all figures in barrels of oil equivalent per day, or BOE/d, using the standard 6:1 Mcf-to-BOE conversion for natural gas. I'll break this down by total production, oil, and gas, highlighting both quarter-over-quarter (QoQ) changes from Q1 2024 and year-over-year (YoY) comparisons to Q2 2023. These results reflect the strength of our high-margin assets, particularly in the Permian Basin, where we've leaned into our multi-bench development strategy.

Starting with the headline: total production averaged 278,000 BOE/d in Q2, up 7% QoQ from 260,000 BOE/d in Q1 and a robust 16% YoY from 240,000 BOE/d in Q2 2023. This marks our strongest quarterly output since the integration of our 2023 Pioneer acquisition—similar to the synergies ExxonMobil realized post their Pioneer deal—and positions us firmly in the upper quartile of peers like Occidental and EOG Resources for growth in the Delaware Basin.

Oil production, our primary driver of free cash flow, came in at 205,000 barrels per day (bbl/d), representing 74% of total BOE. That's a solid 5% QoQ increase from 195,000 bbl/d in Q1 and an impressive 20% YoY jump from 171,000 bbl/d last year. The QoQ lift was propelled by the ramp-up of our initial 12-well pad in the Northern Delaware, where we employed extended laterals averaging 12,500 feet—up from 10,000 feet in prior quarters—coupled with our optimized completion design featuring 2,500 pounds of proppant per foot and diverter technology to enhance cluster efficiency. Initial production rates on these wells averaged 1,800 bbl/d of oil per well in the first 30 days, outperforming our type curve by 15%, thanks to better reservoir quality in the Second Bone Spring interval.

Regionally, the Permian accounted for 85% of our oil volumes, with the Delaware Basin pads contributing over 60% of the QoQ growth. We also saw tailwinds in the Eagle Ford, where oil output rose 8% QoQ to 25,000 bbl/d, driven by two recompletion projects targeting the Lower Eagle Ford shale using dissolvable ball technology, which minimized NPT and boosted EURs by 10-15%. YoY, the oil surge reflects the full-year impact of our 2023 drilling program, where we brought online 85 gross operated wells versus just 62 in Q2 2023, while base declines were limited to 8% organically through proactive workovers and artificial lift optimizations like ESP upgrades with variable frequency drives.

Shifting to natural gas production, we averaged 438,000 Mcf/d, or 73,000 BOE/d equivalent, comprising 26% of total volumes. This delivered a 4% QoQ increase from 421,000 Mcf/d in Q1 and 7% YoY growth from 410,000 Mcf/d. Gas was the standout performer QoQ, benefiting from seasonal demand tailwinds as Henry Hub prices held above $2.80/MMBtu—our realized price of $2.95/MMBtu was up 12% QoQ. Key drivers included gas-rich Second Bone Spring wells in the Delaware, where our GORs stabilized at 1,200 scf/bbl after implementing cyclic pressure drawdowns to manage liquid loading.

That said, gas growth was moderated by strategic curtailments in the Midland Basin, where we voluntarily shut in 15,000 Mcf/d during peak spring flaring season to comply with New Mexico's stringent VOC regulations—echoing challenges faced by ConocoPhillips in the same play. We offset this with third-party midstream expansions, including our joint venture with Crestwood on the Matterhorn Express pipeline, which added 200 MMcf/d of takeaway capacity and reduced basis differentials to under $0.15 below Henry Hub.

Looking at trends and underlying dynamics, our Q2 decline curve flattened to just 7% QoQ, down from 10% in Q1, validating our factory-model approach with simultaneous operations (SIMOPS) across 18 active rigs and three frac crews. Well costs dropped 8% YoQ to $850 per lateral foot in the Permian, driven by supply chain efficiencies on sand and chem additives amid softening service rates—similar to the deflationary pressures Chevron highlighted in their Delaware ops.

On the YoY front, the 16% total growth underscores our capital discipline: we deployed $650 million in Q2 capex, focused 70% on Permian development, yielding a DD&A rate of $12.50/BOE. This compares favorably to peers, with our oil cut expanding to 74% from 71% YoY, enhancing margins as WTI averaged $81/bbl. Challenges included winter weather disruptions in Q1 lingering into early Q2, which deferred 5,000 BOE/d of Eagle Ford gas, and offset volumes from our Bakken divestiture earlier this year—net divestiture impacts were a 2% YoY headwind.

Strategically, these volumes affirm our pathway to 300,000 BOE/d by year-end 2025, with Q3 guidance of 282,000 to 288,000 BOE/d, implying 2-4% sequential growth. We're accelerating Permian inventory conversion with 25% more drilled but uncompleted (DUC) wells entering execution, targeting 110 completions in Q3. ESG-wise, our Permian flaring intensity fell to 1.2%, below state averages, supporting access to capital from investors prioritizing low-carbon operators.

Regionally, the Delaware remains our crown jewel, with 24 months of Tier 1 inventory; Eagle Ford provides counter-cyclical gas uplift; and we're monitoring Bakken for bolt-on M&A post our recent $200 million package sale. In this $75-85 WTI environment, our production mix delivers industry-leading returns—over 60% IRR on new Permian wells—while hedging 55% of Q3 oil at $78/bbl locks in downside protection.

Overall, these results de-risk our full-year target of 275,000-285,000 BOE/d, up 14-19% YoY, and reinforce Apex Energy's position as a Permian pure-play leader.

I will now turn the call over to Sarah Jenkins for an operational update.

Sarah Jenkins: Thank you, John. On the operational front, we continue to execute our strategy effectively. Our production averaged 500,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. We successfully brought several key pads online, which are expected to contribute significantly to our production growth in the coming quarters. We are also making progress on our cost reduction initiatives.

Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. This is Sarah Jenkins, our Executive Vice President of Operations. I'm pleased to dive into our lifting costs per BOE, where we've continued to demonstrate industry-leading discipline and execution. For those unfamiliar, lifting costs—or lease operating expenses, LOE—represent the cash operating costs to produce and maintain each barrel of oil equivalent from our producing assets, excluding royalties, ad valorem taxes, and gathering & transportation. Our focus here has been on driving structural efficiencies while navigating the volatile macro environment, including WTI prices averaging $78 per barrel in Q1 and persistent inflation in steel and tubulars.

Let me start with the trend analysis. Over the past five quarters, we've delivered a compelling downward trajectory in our company-wide lifting costs, reflecting the full impact of our multi-year cost optimization program launched in mid-2022 amid the post-pandemic recovery. Here's the progression:

- Q2 2023: $11.25 per BOE
- Q3 2023: $10.40 per BOE, a 7.5% sequential reduction
- Q4 2023: $9.60 per BOE, down another 7.7%
- Q1 2024: $8.75 per BOE, a further 8.9% decline
- And in Q2 2024, our latest quarter, we've achieved $8.10 per BOE—a 7.4% quarter-over-quarter drop and a cumulative 28% reduction from the Q2 2023 trough.

This puts us in the top quartile of peers, benchmarking favorably against Pioneer Natural Resources' Permian averages around $8-9 per BOE and even outperforming the EIA's reported upstream LOE index, which has hovered flat at ~$10 per BOE industry-wide due to lingering supply chain pressures. Year-to-date, our lifting costs are down 22% YoY, directly contributing over $150 million in free cash flow generation on our 450,000 BOE/d production base.

Regionally, this trend varies by basin but shows consistent improvement across the portfolio:

- Permian Basin (65% of production): Our flagship asset, where Q2 lifting costs fell to $6.80 per BOE—down from $9.20 in Q2 2023. Scale from our 1,200+ active horizontal Delawares and Midland wells, combined with pad drilling efficiencies, has driven this. We're now sub-$7, rivaling EOG Resources' best-in-class metrics.
  
- Eagle Ford (20% of production): $9.50 per BOE in Q2, improved from $12.10 YoY. Legacy vertical wells here benefited from aggressive workover programs, but horizontals are the real story, pulling costs below $8.

- Bakken (10% of production): $11.20 per BOE, down from $14.50. Non-operated assets remain challenged by higher water cut handling, but our operated Mountrail County blocks are at $9.80 thanks to ESP optimizations.

- Gulf of Mexico Shelf (5% of production): $18.40 per BOE, our highest but still down 12% YoY from platform maintenance deferrals. Deepwater pilots remain on hold pending Brent recovery above $80.

Drilling deeper into the drivers, inflationary headwinds like a 15% YoY rise in diesel (key for artificial lift and trucking) and 20% tubular cost escalation were offset by our proactive initiatives. We've executed over 25 targeted cost reduction programs since inception, targeting a $7.50 per BOE run-rate by year-end 2024 and sub-$7 by 2025—positioning us for a $60 WTI floor.

Key technical and operational initiatives delivering this:

1. Predictive Maintenance and Digitalization (20% of savings): Rolled out AI-driven "digital twins" across 70% of our Permian fleet, partnering with Halliburton on their DecisionSpace platform. This has slashed unplanned downtime by 35%, from 4% to 2.6% utilization, avoiding $2.5 million in Q2 workover costs alone. Vibration sensors on 5,000+ rod pumps and ESPs predict failures 14 days in advance, extending run lives from 18 to 28 months.

2. Artificial Lift Optimization (15% of savings): Transitioned 40% of Permian wells from gas lift to variable-speed-drive ESPs, reducing energy consumption by 25%—critical as diesel prices spiked 18% post-Ukraine. In the Bakken, rod pump chemical inhibitors cut paraffin buildup by 50%, deferring $10 million in pulls.

3. Water Management and SWD (Saltwater Disposal) Efficiencies (25% of savings): Handling 4:1 water-oil ratios in the Permian, we've built three new commercial SWD wells with hydraulic fracturing for injectivity, dropping disposal costs from $0.80 to $0.45 per barrel. Recycling initiatives, inspired by Occidental's model, now treat 15% of produced water for frac reuse, saving $18 million YTD.

4. Vendor and Supply Chain Consolidation (18% of savings): Renegotiated frame agreements with Schlumberger and Baker Hughes for 12% LOE discounts on services. Bulk chemical procurement via long-term contracts with Nalco Champion locked in 15% savings amid volatility. Inventory optimization via our ERP system reduced holding costs by $5 million.

5. Electrification and Fuel Switching (12% of savings): Solar-hybrid power on 200 Permian pads, emulating Devon Energy's approach, cut diesel lift fuel by 30%—or $0.40 per BOE. We're targeting 50% electrification by 2026, aligning with Scope 1 emissions goals under the OGCI framework.

6. Workover Prioritization and AFE Discipline (10% of savings): Rigorous AFE gates capped non-routine workovers at $45,000 per job (down from $60k), focusing on high-IRR recompletions in our Dimmit County Eagle Ford shales.

Strategically, these aren't one-offs—they're embedded in our "Permian Plus" framework, leveraging proprietary seismic and machine learning for well spacing down to 400 feet without parent-child interference penalties. This cost trajectory enhances our half-cycle breakevens to $35-40 WTI company-wide, providing resilience amid OPEC+ cuts and potential China demand softness. We're also exploring bolt-on M&A in the Midland Basin, where sub-$7 lifting analogs abound, to accelerate scale.

Looking forward, Q3 guidance holds lifting costs at $7.90-8.30 per BOE, with upside from further ESP rollouts and SWD capacity. Risks include Hurricane season impacting GoM integrity work and potential frac sand inflation, but our hedging covers 60% of diesel exposure.
